articles.title: Why achieving your goals can leave you feeling so empty
articles.author: Stacy Keltner, Chair of the Department of Interdisciplinary Studies and Professor of Philosophy, Kennesaw State University
paras: When Anne Carson learned she had won the Nobel Prize in literature, she was in Iceland, where, according to the Swedish Academy, she was “listening to the wind.”
Carson didn’t answer her phone right away, silencing it until her husband persuaded her to call back. Her verdict on the academy’s choice: “I think you’re all insane.”
Whatever she felt in the moment, there is an irony in Carson’s Nobel win. The highest award in literature has gone to a writer who has spent her career exploring the emptiness of a desire fulfilled.
The honor coincides with the 40th anniversary of the publication of her first book, “Eros the Bittersweet,” a meditation on desire.

In it, Carson argues that desire begins with a void – with wanting what we don’t have. She traces how this feeling of absence shapes love, reading, writing and thinking, activities that renew themselves precisely because they are never complete.
The philosopher and the top

“Eros” begins with a brief preface on Franz Kafka’s “The Top,” a story about a philosopher who spends his time around children so he can chase their spinning tops. When a child sets a top in motion, the philosopher snatches it, believing that understanding any small thing, even a spinning top, would be enough to understand everything.
While the top spins, the philosopher is filled with hope, but as soon as he grasps it, he is repelled by the dumb piece of wood. He throws it down and waits for the next child to spin a top.

For Carson, the story is about why people love to fall in love. The philosopher is after what Carson calls an “impertinent stability in vertigo,” a state that is “itself delightful, a suspended moment of living hope.” The philosopher’s quest for knowledge, Carson cheekily concludes, is simply his pretext for chasing spinning tops. He is enchanted by the spinning itself, and even by his own enchantment – a spell that breaks the instant the top stops in his hand.

Most people know a version of this: There is something animating about chasing a goal. But once attained, the framed degree fades into the wall, the promotion quickly loses its luster, and the plaque becomes another dumb piece of wood.
The delight of wanting disappears in the having.
Why does fulfillment so often feel like loss?

Carson’s answer begins with the Greek word for erotic love, “eros,” which she explains denotes want or lack. Plato’s Socrates makes the same point in the “Symposium.” For the Greeks, no one desires what they already have.

Desire also opens up an absence. To long for someone or something is to discover our own edges, the chasm where the self ends and what is wanted begins. Eros reveals that we are incomplete – an awareness that causes the self to become undone, loosening at the joints.
In one of her poems, the Greek poet Sappho called this experience “glukupikron,” or “sweetbitter.”
Carson’s translation of the passage reads: “Eros once again limb-loosener whirls me / sweetbitter, impossible to fight off, creature stealing up.”

Sappho puts sweet first, Carson notes in “Eros,” but desire is not initially sweet and then bitter. Pleasure and pain arrive together, in the same body and at the same time, before the lover is even able to distinguish them.

Carson extends this pattern to reading, writing and thinking. A reader approaches a text’s meaning but never masters it; every rereading turns up new meanings. The pleasure of understanding and the ache of incompleteness arrive together.

Writing works the same way. A good sentence both captures and conceals what the writer means. Thinking also runs on that doubled feeling, which is how the story of a philosopher chasing tops ended up in a book about love.
The same bittersweet pattern also shows up somewhere far less romantic: at work. Meeting a deadline brings relief that is already hollow because the next one is waiting.

I discovered “Eros the Bittersweet” as a philosophy graduate student, when my goals were to read, write and think my way into questions I loved. Now I spend much of my day as a university administrator, where the quality of my work is measured in metrics and met deadlines. Somewhere along the way, my goals stopped being things I wanted and became things to check off.

Today’s productivity culture chases tops of its own, but it looks less like Kafka’s philosopher than like Lucy and Ethel working at the chocolate factory in the 1952 “I Love Lucy” episode “Job Switching.” As the conveyor belt speeds up, the only way they can look like they’re keeping up is to stuff what they’ve missed into their mouths.

Few things capture this pressure more than the SMART goal. In 1981, management consultant George Doran proposed that goals be SMART: specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. The acronym spread through industries and disciplines as a model for strategic planning, project management, performance evaluations and personal goal-setting. It distills a wider creed: Set the target, sprint after it, hit it. Grasp the top, toss it, capture the next one, ad infinitum. Doran didn’t invent the impulse, but his acronym gave it a checklist.
Carson’s account of desire helps explain why this creed leads to two kinds of emptiness.

The first comes from pursuing goals people never really desired. Inbox zero and a quarterly metric are goals in service of goals, the ultimate of which is productivity itself, which often simply ends up boosting someone else’s productivity.

The second comes from goals people truly wanted. Psychologist Tal Ben-Shahar calls the letdown that follows the “arrival fallacy” – the belief that reaching a destination will bring lasting happiness.

The Greeks offer another kind of striving, one that locates pleasure in the pursuit itself rather than in the prize. In Plato’s “Phaedrus,” Socrates describes eros as giving the soul wings and treats philosophy as a love of wisdom no one can own.

Centuries later, philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre distinguished external goods, such as money and status, from goods internal to a practice, such as a farmer’s growing mastery of her land or an architect’s pursuit of elegant, functional design. MacIntyre’s example, in his 1981 book “After Virtue,” is a child paid in candy to learn chess. As long as she plays for the candy, she has every reason to cheat. Only when she comes to love the game does she gain what chess itself can give: a particular kind of analytical skill, strategic imagination and competitive intensity.
To Socrates, MacIntyre and Carson, external goods get used up as they are won. Internal goods deepen the longer we pursue them.

Keeping desire alive means choosing pursuits that can never be finished – a craft, a field of study, a relationship – and letting the gap between reaching and grasping stay open. In this way, the lack that can hollow us out can also be what moves us.

Carson was handed the highest prize in literature. Yet the picture the Swedish Academy left us with is of a writer standing in the Icelandic wind, attending to a force of nature that no one can catch.

articles.title: Silence of the Lambs: Hannibal Lecter makes his stage debut in this inventive touring production
articles.author: Christina Wilkins, Lecturer in Film and Creative Writing, University of Birmingham
paras: When you think of the serial killer and former forensic psychiatrist Hannibal Lecter, what comes to mind?

I would bet good money it’s Anthony Hopkins in Jonathan Demme’s 1991 film Silence of the Lambs, talking about eating someone’s liver with fava beans and a nice chianti. This film, an adaptation of Robert Harris’s book of the same name, projected the character into the cultural zeitgeist.

There have been multiple adaptations of Harris’s four novels about Lecter since the first, Red Dragon, was released in 1981. These include Manhunter (1989), the Hannibal film (2001), Red Dragon (2002), the NBC series Hannibal (2013 to 2015), and more recently, a television series Clarice (2021), focusing on the events of The Silence of the Lambs.
Lecter now makes his stage debut in an adaptation of The Silence of the Lambs.

Much like the film, this adaptation sees FBI trainee Clarice Starling sent to interview cannibal sociopath Dr Hannibal Lecter at the behest of her mentor, Jack Crawford. Crawford hopes that Lecter can shed some light on a recent spate of serial killings where women are being flayed by Buffalo Bill (real name Jame Gumb) to make a skin suit. In the conversations between Lecter and Clarice, an uneasy connection emerges. Clarice must find Bill’s latest victim, Catherine Martin, before time runs out.

Before going to see this adaptation, I wondered whether there would be any imitation of the visual elements of the film. Specifically, would there be a repetition of characteristics that came to define the character of Hannibal specifically?

There are moments of this throughout: the look of the cell and the mask, the slicked back hair and demeanour of Hannibal (played here by John Partridge), the night-vision goggles of the showdown between Buffalo Bill (Sam Jackson) and Clarice (Mollie Gallagher). This is perhaps necessary. Adaptations often bring with them what literary critic Linda Hutcheon calls “knowing audiences” who are familiar with the text and therefore may look for and want similarities.
Moving from the mediums the story has previously inhabited (novel, film, television) to stage offers the opportunity for new ways to tell this story, which the production takes advantage of.

The staging is impressive, neatly segueing between the asylum where Lecter is kept, the FBI training school Quantico, Jack Crawford’s (Oliver Farnworth) office and Buffalo Bill’s house where he holds women captive before killing them. The production’s switching between these settings feels smooth and characters inhabit mixed worlds in the storytelling. One notable sequence saw Buffalo Bill sitting atop Lecter’s cage sewing his skin suit while Clarice and Lecter discussed him. In this, Bill is physically and metaphorically hovering over them.

The production also employs interesting techniques to give the audience information in unique ways. These included the projection of the case files of a patient being discussed across the dark of the stage. Another is the screening of a press conference by Catherine Martin’s (Lottie Amor) mother (Jo Mousley) projected onto a fine screen across the stage, which becomes more transparent, allowing the audience to see events on the stage as she speaks. This multiplicity of action capitalises on the opportunities of theatre, and avoids any moment or storyline feeling too static.
One notable, and welcome, change is the characterisation of Buffalo Bill. In Demme’s 1991 film, the portrayal was seen as queerphobic and transphobic, leading to protests from activist groups.

As one leader of the LGBTQ+ media rights group Glaad commented at the time: “He has a poodle named Precious, he sews, he wears a nipple ring, he has an affected feminine voice, and he cross-dresses. He completely promotes homophobia.” (In more recent years, the portrayal has been recast as transphobia.)
The 1994 film Philadelphia, about the mistreatment of a gay man dying of Aids, is often viewed as a form of apology to the LGBTQ+ community for Silence.

This new theatre production, however, steps back from the controversy of the film. Instead, Bill is presented as childlike, often sitting cross-legged like at school, or roaming around the stage in his underwear (representing, in part, his “unfinished” nature).

John Partridge clearly relishes playing Hannibal Lecter, pacing around the stage in a catlike way. Aside from a few vocal echoes of Hopkins in his delivery – for instance, in the way he says “F…B…I” and “Quid pro quo, Clarice” – Partridge manages to offer a take on the character that avoids mimicry. His portrayal changes the physicality of Lecter, adds more energy than the template that Hopkins provided.

Similarly, Mollie Gallagher’s Clarice retains echoes of Foster in her voice, with the husky tones and approach to the accent strikingly similar. Maybe this is because Hopkins’s Hannibal mocks the background and West Virginian (Appalachian) accent in the film, imitating it while asking: “What is your father, dear? Is he a coal miner?”
The characters’ relationship is also altered on stage by their physical proximity to one another, developing more of a closeness and tension, which is absent in other adaptations.

The production overall gives some moments that re-address some of the concerns of previous adaptations. For instance, Buffalo Bill’s victim Catherine Martin. It delivers elements of familiarity for audiences, while allowing for subtle tweaks that reframe Harris’ text.

There are some commendable decisions here in adapting the screen to the stage. However, is it the most novel and inventive adaptation? Possibly not. But as a fan of Hannibal Lecter it was fun to see how this story could come alive in the theatre and I’m sure other fans will enjoy it too. For those who are new to the story, it still presents an engaging piece of theatre well worth seeing.
The Silence of the Lambs is running on a major UK and Ireland tour from October 2026 through to June 2027

articles.title: Hauntology examines how what happened in the past – and what didn’t – informs the present
articles.author: Robert Edgar, Professor of Writing and Popular Culture, York St John University
paras: The spooky is a hugely popular phenomenon in British culture, demonstrated in what now seems like a month-long Halloween celebration, a rich tradition of horror cinema and a growing interest in the uncanny. But, there are other manifestations of haunting.

At York St John University, the Hauntology and Spectrality Research Group explores the ways in which the past continues to shape literature, film and all other aspects of contemporary culture and everyday life.

Drawing upon philosophy, cultural theory, media studies, literature, health care and sociology, our group examines how traces of what we might think has disappeared often remain present in subtle and unexpected ways. Our work is concerned with ghosts, not in the conventional supernatural sense, but rather with the broader question of how absence can nevertheless exert a powerful presence.

Central to our research is the concept of hauntology, a term introduced by French philosopher Jacques Derrida in Specters of Marx (1993). Hauntology challenges the assumption that the past can ever be fully left behind. Instead it suggests that histories, memories, ideas and unrealised possibilities linger within the present, shaping contemporary experience.

Closely related is the concept of spectrality, which examines the ways in which absent people, places, cultures and futures continue to make themselves felt – what sociologist Avery Gordon described as Ghostly Matters (1997).

Spectres, in this sense, are not necessarily paranormal entities, but the traces of things that refuse to disappear completely. It is what the highly influential critic Mark Fisher describes as a “a failure of absence or a failure of presence” in his book The Weird and the Eerie (2016).

Over the past two decades, hauntology and spectrality have continued to become increasingly influential within both academic and popular culture. Scholars apply these concepts to subjects as diverse as literature, architecture, politics, heritage, technology, criminology, landscape, photography and media.

At the same time, wider public interest in themes of nostalgia, memory, folklore and cultural loss has grown significantly, as is clear from the number of events around the country, including public talks on the history of folk horror and our own York Society of Hauntologists reading group.

From the resurgence of interest in folk horror and forgotten histories to contemporary discussions of nostalgia and heritage, many cultural phenomena can be understood as responses to the persistence of the past within the present.
Britain as a haunted country
The research group investigates how these hauntological dynamics operate across a range of cultural contexts. We are particularly interested in questions of memory, place and identity.

How do landscapes retain the traces of previous lives and histories? Why do certain buildings, objects or cultural forms evoke such powerful feelings of presence and absence? How do communities remember what has been lost, and how do those memories continue to shape collective identities? These questions sit at the heart of our interdisciplinary approach.

Britain provides a particularly rich context for this work. It is a nation characterised by layers of history. It is a country where Roman roads, medieval churches, industrial ruins and contemporary developments coexist within the same spaces. In these terms, the past is not experienced as something distant but as something embedded within everyday life.

Hauntology offers a valuable framework for understanding these encounters between different times and histories. Often the past haunts us from a much closer place, something we explored in relation to the resurgence of interest in folk horror and in the interest in the 1970s and 1980s as a site of cultural production.

People who experienced childhood in the last three decades of the 20th century are what the cultural critic Bob Fischer describes as “the haunted generation” – something that is explored in Horrifying Children an anthology which I co-authored and edited in 2024.

In this book, academics describe the interest in the the TV of our youth as much more than cosy nostalgia. Instead it is a place where “revisiting these texts then becomes a seance of sorts, where adults seek to commune with past selves and past experiences”.

Hauntological enquiry also considers the relationship between haunting and the future. One of the most important contributions of hauntological theory is its emphasis on unrealised possibilities. The present is haunted not only by what has happened but also by what failed to happen – these are characterised as lost futures.

The application of the ideas associated with hauntology and spectrality are growing all the time. Our medical hauntology sub-group is exploring the application of these ideas in medical settings for both practitioners and patients.

While Britain has provided a useful focus, our members represent countries from all around the world, all with specific application of these ideas. This is something reflected in the Spectres, Hauntings and Horrors book series.

Ultimately, the work of the Hauntology and Spectrality Research Group is driven by a simple but important focus: memories endure, histories resurface, places retain traces of former lives, and forgotten possibilities continue to shape our understanding of the world. So enjoy the spooky season while it is upon us, but don’t forget that you are haunted all year round.

articles.title: Raye’s ambitious Mercury Prize-winning album is a testament to female creative freedom
articles.author: Eva Dieteren, PhD researcher in Gender and Popular Music, Kingston University
paras: Making an album might seem like a strange project in an age of streaming, when so many listeners rarely listen to albums from start to finish.

For Raye, however, the album is not merely a selection of individual singles: it is a piece of highly personal storytelling. This Music May Contain Hope – the album that won her the Mercury Prize – is a one-hour-and-13-minute magnum opus. It sweeps from old-Hollywood jazz and big-band productions to cinematic orchestral flourish, guided by a voice that is by turns conversational and theatrical. It is a musical statement of what Raye can do when given free rein.

As she says by way of introduction in Girl Under The Grey Cloud, “allow me to set the scene”. It is 2023, and after seven long years of struggling to convince her former label to let her release an album, Raye independently releases her debut album, My 21st Century Blues.

Three years later, she has taken home the coveted Mercury Prize for her follow-up, This Music May Contain Hope. “Being able to even create an album is a privilege I will never take for granted”, she wrote on Instagram (below), posting a selfie that shows the singer smiling as she clutched her golden trophy at the awards show in Newcastle on October 22.

Over 17 tracks on the album, Raye directs a genre-bending musical experience that is anything but minimalist. The production is opulent, with lush brass, layered vocals and even includes voice notes from Raye’s loved ones. Its most ambitious moment is Click Clack Symphony, a spectacular collaboration with film composer Hans Zimmer, bringing together emotional release with a cinematic soundscape.

Seeing Raye as a creative director does not mean she is a lone genius. Like any director, she leads a cast and crew, and she makes sure that her fans know who they are. She offers a heartfelt introduction to soul legend Al Green on Goodbye Henry, and at the end of I Hate The Way I Look Today, she sends the band off with the affectionate line: “alright everyone, have a cup of tea now.”

These personal little asides and reverential mentions all go in the mix as part of the singer’s M.O. On the six-minute-long closing track Fin, Raye names every contributor to the album. It is a rare gesture in pop, where credits usually stay hidden in the small print.

But what marks Raye out as a creative director is her insistence on contrast. On I Hate The Way I Look Today, raw, confessional lines about body image are set against the glamour of an old Hollywood big-band arrangement. And The WhatsApp Shakespeare, whose title alone pairs the modern with the classic, opens on a contemporary R&B beat before bursting into up-tempo swing and ending with James Bond-esque music that fades into a haunting outro.

By bringing the old and the new together, Raye shows us what makes up her musical DNA, as well as her respect for musical tradition. But she does it without slipping into nostalgia; rather, she pushes it into something new.

Raye is, without a doubt, an incredible vocalist. What is most remarkable, though, is not just her ability to belt out tunes, but the range of vocal styles she uses on the album. From operatic highs to soulful ad-libs and playful scatting, it is the way she uses her voice that directs listeners through the melodrama of her stories.

Reviewers of her live shows have criticised her “tendency to overshare” in long spoken passages between songs. On the album, however, these spoken moments have a clear purpose. On Beware.. The South London Lover Boy, she sets the scene as a narrator, opening with a prologue in a distinctly posh accent, warning us about its title character.

When I first heard the opening of Nightingale Lane – “This is a song about the greatest heartbreak I’ve ever known” – I was struck by the boldness of the confession, bracing myself for the catharsis that was coming.

Like the title character of comedy-drama Fleabag, Raye’s spoken intros and outros break the fourth wall, creating a sense of intimacy with her listeners. The result is an album that is conceptually rich and musically bold yet vulnerable and therapeutic. But Raye’s vulnerability is never self-absorbed. She turns it outwards, offering a final promise to the listener on Happier Times Ahead before the credits roll: “Just hold on to happier times, alright darlin’?”

Some critics have found the result “overstuffed with musical ideas” and at times “over-indulgent and messy”. Yet I hear an artist making full use of the freedom long denied to her, and to many women in music.

Increasingly, women are seizing creative control of their music. Some of the most acclaimed albums of recent years have been ambitious, story-driven records by women. Most prominently, these include Beyoncé’s 2025 Grammy-winning Cowboy Carter, a reclamation of the black female lineage in country music, and Rosalía’s Lux, a stunning meditation on female divinity sung in 13 languages.
These artists are not only powerful vocalists and performers, but creative directors of conceptually rich musical worlds. On This Music May Contain Hope, Raye claims that role for herself.

articles.title: Beyond Hokusai’s Great Wave – what to see and read this week
articles.author: Naomi Joseph, Arts + Culture Editor, The Conversation
paras: Katsushika Hokusai’s Great Wave is possibly one of the most celebrated works in art history, But did you know it’s part of a much larger series?

Look closely and you will see framed by the great frothing crested wave is Japan’s Mount Fuji. The Great Wave, which is actually titled Under the Wave off Kanagawa, is only one of 46 of Hokusai’s Views of Mount Fuji, created between 1830 and 1834. You can see them all for the first time in the UK at London’s Dulwich Picture Gallery.

Across the series, Hokusai depicts the mountain from varying viewpoints, times of year and day, and across moments in people’s lives. You’ll see Mount Fuji on a clear day, in the distance from a street lined with shops, from the perspective of people on a pilgrimage and from the balcony of a temple.

Our reviewer Dominik Havsteen-Franklin was moved by how much his relationship with the Great Wave was altered by seeing it as one in a whole series. When he looked at the wave and the mighty Fuji looking tiny in the distance, he thought of the people working at its base and living in the villages surrounding it. He realised how the mountain’s colour would change if Hokusai had painted it at a different time of year. Ultimately, he was left with was an ever-greater appreciation for this important work.
Hokusai: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from the Iuchi Collection is on at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, until January 17 2027

Elsewhere in London, another first is happening: the solo show of the Colombian figurative artist Fernando Botero. The exhibition, Fernando Botero, in Praise of an Amplified World, presents a range of paintings and sculptures from across the artist’s extraordinary 70-year career.

There is something pleasing about the rotundness of Botero’s people. Squat and sturdy, they swell to fill the canvas or burst from their bronze edges with all their fleshy humanity. Botero’s approach to scale and volume, compressing and expanding at once, is incredibly playful and his use of colour is just so inviting.

I particularly love his paintings of women in which they are presented looking like heavily ornamented multi-tier cakes, like En La Plaza (1987). When you see them, you may find yourself wondering if British artist Beryl Cook drew on the influence of the Columbian painter.

Those who know Botero for such whimsical works might be surprised by those painted with the same sensibility depicting grim scenes of violence. Or paintings which come with a serious political message, such as the rotund police-like figures dragging away a bloodied dead bull. It’s an exhibition that reveals the breadth and depth of this immensely skilled artist’s work.
Fernando Botero, in Praise of an Amplified World is at the Opera Gallery, London until November 22

Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK at The William Morris Gallery in London explores how people, places and communities have shaped ideas of home, art and activism in Britain over the past 200 years. Featuring artworks, photographs and archival materials, it highlights unconventional homes and the radical individuals who challenged social norms, while examining how class and wealth influence access to alternative ways of living.

You’ll see historic homes like William Morris’s Red House in London and the Bloomsbury Group’s Sussex home Charleston, but also Danièle Lamarche’s 1980s photographs of Bangladeshi squatters in east London. Our reviewer found the exhibition a profound exploration of the myriad struggles and joys that have shaped modern life.
Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK is on at The William Morris Gallery, London, until March 28 2027
Keeping women’s stories alive
Phillipa Gregory’s new book Royal Witch retells the story of Eleanor Cobham, “the woman they called witch. Who would have called herself queen”.

Cobham, like many women before and after her, suffered for being ambitious and wanting to improve her lot in life. The 15th-century Englishwoman rose from modest beginnings to the highest ranks of society when she married the Duke of Gloucester, briefly heir presumptive to the throne. How did she get there? Sorcery and witchcraft, if you believe the formal inquiry. For this, she was paraded barefoot throught the streets of London and then imprisoned for life.

Gregory’s book keeps the story alive, letting us not forget how horribly history treated women. Historian Lynsey Cowlishaw asks us to approach such stories critically, and examine the facts and nuance that are conveniently overlooked when a powerful woman is reduced to her reputation as a witch.
Royal Witch by Phillipa Gregory is out now

Talking of keeping stories alive, UK publisher Persephone Books’ mission is just that. The publisher is helping to bring “lost” 20th-century novels by women to 21st century bookshelves. Its latest is Her Son’s Wife by Dorothy Canfield Fisher.

You’ve likely never heard of the book or its author, unless you are already a Persephone fan. However, in her heyday Canfield Fisher was a household name and Her Son’s Wife was tipped to win the Pulitzer prize when it was first published in 1926.

The book tells the story of Mrs Mary Bascomb, a woman in her mid-40s who thought all the tumult of life was behind her. That is till the rhythms of her quiet domestic world are interrupted when her son unexpectedly returns home from college with a new wife.

Mary finds herself on the defensive as her lovingly maintained home is increasingly taken over by the young couple. It is a wonderful, gentle book that our reviewer says beautifully captures the quiet magic and emotion of domestic life.
Her Son’s Wife by Dorothy Canfield Fisher is out now

articles.title: Booker prize 2026: a diverse list to inspire all sorts of readers – six experts review the nominees
articles.author: Tory Young, Associate Professor in Department of English Literature, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: When the Booker prize was first launched in 1969, its aim was to get more people reading and to stimulate discussion about contemporary literature. Now, we all know reading is at an all time low but there really has never been a better time to reignite your love of fiction and to discover (or rediscover) your love of reading. And, this year’s shortlist is really a testament to the breadth of stories available out there.

There’s poetic historic fiction with May we Feed the King about a reluctant medieval king from Rebecca Perry. For lovers of science fiction, M. John Harrison has written a tale about aliens and social collapse set on the Kentish coast. And, there’s laughter to be found in Black Bag by Luke Kennard about an out-of-work actor who lands a gig in a psychological experiment.

There are also new works by previous winners and nominees. Marlon James is back with a startling portrait of the lives of gay men in Jamaica. Douglas Stuart gives us his chilly Hebridean family drama, John of John. And, finally there’s the gentle political commentary of Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say about what happens when good people stay quiet.
Ahead of the prize being announced on November 9, we’ve asked six experts to guide you through the nominations for 2026.

Black Bag was inspired by a 1967 experiment at Oregon State University in which an individual cloaked in black sat mutely in a seminar for a semester. Where the study focused on the reactions of the witnesses, Black Bag is the story and meditations of the man who becomes increasingly attached to his role and, amusingly, his bag.

Kennard’s protagonist is a flat-broke actor relying on cash-in-hand corporate murder mysteries and the kindness of his friend Claudio in an otherwise dismal world. Wearing the bag outside of the classroom not only removes the problem of how to be but even attracts the attention of a female professor who wants “to fuck nothing” – he is both strikingly visible and anonymous. The novel is laugh-out-loud funny but melancholy and provocative too. Some of Bag’s strongest relationships are those he imagines, like ongoing conversations with his parents’ dog and narrated village life with a fictional Swedish wife.
By Tory Young, associate professor in English literature
The End of Everything by M. John Harrison

The backdrop of The End of Everything is alien invasion, but treated with a ludic contempt for genre conventions. An ineffectual war is being waged against the sardonically named iGhetti – amorphous entities who have leaked into the world “from the astral plane”. Phillip Tennent, a beachcomber somewhere on the Kent coast, finds an iGhetti artefact washed up by the tide, a thing that slowly begins to ape humanity, an event which throws Tennent’s life and the life of his ageing, forgetful aunt, Marnie, into brutality and random violence.

In his 2023 “anti-memoir”, Wish I Was Here, M. John Harrison writes of his world-building: “I’d rather pile up real facts to reveal something evidently unreal than pile up invented facts to make something unreal seem real.” The real facts pile up here – cheek by jowl with dense allusion and the surreal – into a work of slippery unreality, which is nevertheless congested with raw feeling and startling poetry.
Tim Jarvis, senior lecturer in creative writing
The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Elizabeth Strout’s slight book is a series of snapshot insights into the thoughts and memories of protagonist, Massachusetts Bay high school History teacher Artie Dam. With Artie at the centre, it captures the problems, relationships, and futures of a community: extended family, students, colleagues, whose lives connect unexpectedly, or are influenced by brief interactions – statements of support or honesty. Sometimes, Artie worries he lies through kindness; he isn’t to know that his positivity manifests unexpected joys.
Nominated for the prize three times before, Pulitzer-winner Strout’s elegant text is both melancholic and evocative.

Measured, thoughtful, and good, Artie Dam is caught up in political, socioeconomic, personal, and philosophical questions threatening to derail his life. These also bring him closer to people he loves, including his son Rob and his extravagant, reckless friend, Flossie. Artie clings on to the possibility of free will while the reader hopes that everything will work out well for Artie.
Jenni Ramone, associate professor of postcolonial and global literature
The Disappearers by Marlon James
The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive.

The action begins as eight men gather to rehearse John Herbert’s provocative and unsettling 1967 US prison play Fortune and Men’s Eyes about homosexuality and sexual power play. A homophobic mob storms a rehearsal and by the end of the evening, one man is murdered and another blinded. Shortly afterwards, two disappear. Six years later, the search for the disappeared continues and the novel makes it clear that gay men in Jamaica disappear way before anyone notices they’ve gone.

In Marlon’s writing of their differences in class, ethnicity, social privilege, sexual preference, desire for attachment, emotional intelligence, eloquence, and identity constructions, the novel writes away the enforced flatness of slurs and stereotypes of gay men to humanise at scale. It’s an everyday act of narrative restitution that has revolutionary significance given the continuing sexual politics of Jamaica.
Alison Donnell, professor of modern literature
John of John by Douglas Stuart

An omniscient narrator presides over John of John as we follow John-Calum Macleod – Cal – a recent Edinburgh art school grad, who has been studying fashion and textiles. Learning that his maternal grandmother Ella is ill, Cal is persuaded to return home by his lay-preacher father, John, during one of their weekly phone calls.

Once home, we’re witness to the claustrophobic dysfunction of the Macleods’ home, a small croft where John rears sheep, weaves tweed, and has strong connections to the “Wee Free” church. John struggles to show anything other than contempt towards his son, who has come home with growing debt and orange hair.

As a young gay man hailing from a strict and repressive Free Presbyterian background, Cal remains still in the closet as far as his island is concerned. The torment and guilt of his sexuality weigh heavily on Cal throughout the novel.

The drama and (sometimes verging on implausible) twists of this book make it feel like a soap opera, in the traditional sense of the term: small, interconnected characters and high melodrama, with domestic spaces as scenes of desire, revelation and unpredictability. But this is not a criticism. Stuart’s lyrical prose and atmospheric narrative elevate the genre – reimagining the domestic and familial tropes by focusing on the unrequited affections of the men in the story.
Stevie Marsden, lecturer in publishing
May We Feed The King by Rebecca Perry

This is a poet’s novel, without the seductive immersion more usual for those on the Booker shortlist. In three parts, the first and last are narrated by a person – their sex is never given – whose job is creating food scenes in historical sites. Following a never specified tragedy, they are commissioned to create a tableaux in a former palace. In the archive they come across a page detailing the failings of a medieval king. The middle part of the novel is that king’s story.

While the narrator’s work is about bringing the past close, the novel itself is an exercise in distance. We are told very little about the tableaux maker; the characters in the middle section are known only by their roles.

This distance enacts the novel’s central questions about history and storytelling, but it is not a cold distance. The novel is full of passages of beauty and delight. The narrator’s description of a website that sells replica food made me laugh and took my breath away.
Leigh Wilson, professor of English literature

articles.title: Wicker and the rise of the ‘monster romance’: why audiences are falling for the non-human
articles.author: Natalie Wall, PhD Candidate in English Literature, University of Liverpool
paras: Wicker is an unorthodox love story from husband-and-wife filmmaking team Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Based on Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story, The Wicker Husband, it blends satirical folk fable with elements of the modern rom-com.

The film, set vaguely in the middle ages, follows a lonely fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband made from wicker (Alexander Skarsgård). Ultimately she falls in love with her handmade companion.

Colman’s fisherwoman is pitied for her unmarried status which is believed, at least in part, to stem from her perpetual fishy stench, prompting ridicule from the villagers. However, set against the comically bad marriages of those around her, she doesn’t seem to be in such a bad position, highlighting that, under patriarchy, women are damned if they do and damned if they don’t.

The addition of a preternaturally devoted wicker husband to the village creates a new benchmark for marriage – one that stirs and intrigues the women and profoundly worries the men. It’s a bawdy yet astute exploration of what it means to challenge the heterosexual status quo.

Wicker arrives amid a remarkable boom in stories centred around relationships between the human and non-human. Monsters, aliens, dragons, demons and even household objects have increasingly moved from the margins of fantasy culture into the centre of popular romantic storytelling.

Films such as Lisa Frankenstein and A Useful Ghost have recently attracted smaller cult fan followings. And earlier successes including The Shape of Water, Warm Bodies and Edward Scissorhands have helped establish the idea that unconventional romantic partners can carry emotionally resonant mainstream narratives.
What has changed is not simply audience tolerance for the strange. Instead, our cultural ideas about intimacy, desire and romance are being reimagined.

Stories of humans forming relationships with beings they’ve made or transformed appear throughout mythology and folklore. Perhaps the most well-known example is the Greek myth of Pygmalion, in which a sculptor falls in love with Galatea, a statue of a beautiful woman that is brought to life.

There are countless other examples: stories appear in Jewish legends about beings made of clay called golems; northern European folktales tell of the selkies which can shapeshift between seal and human forms by removing or putting on their seal skins. And a whole multitude of fairytales hinge on magical transformations. Such narratives ask enduring questions about what makes someone human, what constitutes life and whether love can overcome radical physical differences.

Wicker’s romantic hero is clearly part of this long genealogy of made, crafted or transformed partners. But the character, while not necessarily or strictly monstrous, also speaks to the rising interest in “monster romance” within the rapidly expanding romance and romantasy book market.
Romantasy has become one of the publishing industry’s most successful genres and within it, readers have enthusiastically embraced relationships that cross species boundaries.

Katee Robert’s bestselling The Dragon’s Bride follows a relationship between a woman and a dragon-like being and Ruby Dixon’s wildly popular Ice Planet Barbarians series has crafted an entire romantic saga between various women and aliens from a frozen planet.

Monster romance fans have carved out their own niche on platforms like Instagram and, perhaps most significantly, TikTok’s BookTok, where they passionately champion their favourite books, couples and monster romance tropes.

Many of these books originated outside traditional publishing. Lauren Roberts’ Powerless and Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Soul Of Ash And Blood were propelled by reader-driven recommendation networks and algorithmic infrastructure.

Communities like BookTok helped self-published authors build dedicated audiences long before major publishers recognised the commercial potential of the trend. As a result, stories once regarded as too strange or specialised for mainstream audiences are now bestsellers and the cultural appetite for the unusual has grown.

The popularity of monster romance has prompted critics to ask why readers are increasingly drawn to non-human partners. One explanation is that these narratives create distance from familiar romantic conventions.

By removing relationships from recognisable social realities, writers gain space to explore intimacy in new ways. Monster romances often challenge assumptions about things like beauty and gender expectations. The central conflict is rarely whether the monster is worthy of love; in fact, the stories frequently present the non-human figure as unusually attentive, loyal and emotionally available.

This dynamic has led some critics to connect the popularity of monster romance to “heteropessimism”: a growing cultural sense that conventional heterosexual relationships feel disappointing, unequal or exhausted.

Rather than abandoning romance altogether, audiences may be searching for alternative ways of imagining sexuality and emotional fulfilment. Here the monster becomes a vehicle for exploring possibilities outside of the patriarchal heterosexual partnership. (However, it must be noted that many of these romances are still broadly heterosexual, despite their play with gender roles and expression.)

But Wicker doesn’t just feature a non-human lover; he’s also a man-made one. Within our climate of heteropessimism and dating despair, stories about creating our ideal partner feel even more relevant. They examine the relationship between creation and desire, as well as asking what happens when people attempt to manufacture intimacy rather than discover it.

Digital technologies increasingly mediate romantic relationships. Dating apps encourage people to sort through seemingly endless options of potential partners while profiting from users’ desire for connection. And AI chat bots have introduced new discussions about the nature of companionship and the potential for relationships with digital beings.

Against this backdrop, the wicker husband embodies contemporary anxieties about loneliness and connection while also offering a fantasy of uncomplicated and unwavering devotion. The film emerges from a cultural landscape already primed for stories about loving the strange, the constructed and the non-human.

articles.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
articles.author: Karrin Vasby Anderson, Professor of Communication Studies, Colorado State University
paras: Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views.
But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture, from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.

Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media. The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan. Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” spark controversy and turn into political footballs, while late-night talk show hosts must skirt the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor.

While we know a lot about the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats, there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas. This is particularly true for younger people, who are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources.

Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities. She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making.

As co-founders and research affiliates of Colorado State University’s Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture, we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49.

We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content.

That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell. And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity.
Favorite influencers and podcasts
Pop culture is the diverse collection of cultural productions consumed by members of a society: films, television series, video games, art, music, comedy and the like.
We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series. We examined results by age and political party.

Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category. The answers were diffuse, but trends are evident in the top three listed by people across political affiliations.
Both the Democratic and Republican parties have turned to influencers to reach voters – particularly young voters – who “don’t consume traditional political news.”

In our survey’s lists of favorite influencers, three creators who rose to fame staging viral stunts, interviewing celebrities and playing video games on YouTube and the live streaming platform Twitch dominated the list: MrBeast was No. 1 for Democrats, Republicans and independents. Republicans and independents ranked Kai Cenat in their top three, while IShowSpeed was No. 2 for Democrats and Republicans.

A similar pattern of the same names populating each list is evident in people’s favorite podcasts. “The Joe Rogan Experience” and “Call Her Daddy” were in all groups’ top three, while Republicans and independents also ranked the “Tucker Carlson Show” and “This Past Weekend with Theo Von.”

Joe Rogan and Theo Von are comedians turned podcasters, whereas Tucker Carlson rose to fame as a right-wing pundit. “Call Her Daddy” is an outlier on our list insofar as it is hosted by a woman, Alex Cooper, and is known for frank discussions of sex and relationships.

The website Campaigns & Elections reported that in 2024 half of all registered voters surveyed who listened to at least one podcast per month said that podcasts had some influence on their vote. The site reported that in the 2024 presidential election, those podcast listeners favored conservatives.

Our survey helps to explain why. Rogan, popular with all three groups, has long voiced libertarian ideas and platformed right-wing politicians. Von occupies a similar space, and Carlson is conservative. Both are favorites not just of Republicans but also independents.
Favorite comedians and video games
Political scientists and media scholars have demonstrated how comedy can influence politics. Our survey found considerable overlap among political partisans’ favorite comedians.

Dave Chappelle, creator of the boundary-breaking Comedy Central series “Chappelle’s Show,” topped the list for Democrats and Republicans and was the second favorite of independents. Bill Burr, known for comedy that is both cocky and aggrieved, was in the top three for Republicans and Democrats, while Shane Gillis, whose comedy The New York Times says “fits into the evolving meaning of conservatism,” was second and third for independents and Republicans.

Video games are another shared pop culture venue where Americans of different political affiliations are encountering one another as they play, via discussions with other players on Twitch and by participating in the comments sections of gameplay livestreams.

Researchers have demonstrated that young people, in particular, are exposed to diverse political views when engaging with one another in “online participatory activities that are non-political in nature.”

For example, one study examined how a viral trend of “building Trump’s wall” while playing Fortnite spurred political discussions both inside the game and in comments on gameplay videos and social media posts.

U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demonstrated the political power of the medium in 2020 when she livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us, an online, multiplayer deduction game similar to the popular party games Mafia and Werewolf. Ocasio-Cortez playing the game with U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and prominent gamers was billed as a get-out-the-vote effort and earned 4.5 million views.
In our survey of video games favored by people of different political affiliations, Call of Duty, Fortnite and Sims appeared on all three lists.
Our data suggests that these pop culture spaces are thus not partisan silos. But that doesn’t mean they are free of particular ideologies.

Some of the most popular creators – Rogan, Von, Carlson and Gillis – appeal to, or helped construct, the manosphere, a loose collection of online communities that promote masculinity and often reflect misogynistic attitudes.
Burr’s comedy is not politically conservative. But The New York Times said that it “gives voice to the aggrieved confusion of the white heterosexual guy adrift.”

Chappelle is known for his satirical critiques of racism. But in his more recent Netflix stand-up specials, he voiced anti-trans sentiments that Mother Jones called “indistinguishable from, and grist for, the material of conservative streamers and right-wing edgelords.”

Our survey did not ask respondents why they preferred these influencers, podcasts, comedians and video games. Academic research has shown that pop culture audiences don’t passively accept every message a creator delivers. Nevertheless, the dominance of male creators and the prevalence of misogyny and transphobia in their humor and commentary is significant.

Whether convened online or in person, the groups that gather via popular culture do not fit into the partisan silos that have formed around news and social media outlets. That makes the gendered nature of these lists even more significant, because the manosphere vibes are not relegated to one side of the political spectrum.

articles.title: The Black designers redefining British fashion by drawing on their own heritage, culture and history
articles.author: Andrew Ibi, Programme Leader BA Fashion: Design & Communication, School of Art and Creative Industries, Liverpool John Moores University
paras: British fashion has always been shaped by creative exchange: forged inside melting pots, authored by radical style communities – and often fuelled by class and migration.

Over the past decade, we’ve witnessed the distinct emergence of a new genre centred on the Black British experience. It has seen its designers drawing on their unique histories, the most prominent of which are Martine Rose, Priya Ahluwalia, Nicholas Daley, Bianca Saunders, Saul Nash and Grace Wales Bonner, with the latter appointed to lead Hermès menswear in 2025.
The story is evolving. A new wave of talent is developing its own visual languages, challenging notions of Britishness and the expectation of what Black fashion design should look like.
At London Fashion Week in September 2026, Francesca Lake presented Wake the Town, a spectacular exploration of Jamaican funeral traditions, nuanced dress forms and their cultural contradictions.

Lake is developing an immersive design language that celebrates cultural memory and contemporary invention. The Jamaican-born, London-based designer is skilfully disrupting historical style notes to subvert ruffled lace crinolines and elaborate church headwear while purposing theatrical silhouettes into a distorted proposal of British identity.

Joshua Ewusie, founder of E.W.USIE, is busy transforming everyday cultural references into luxurious and sophisticated fashion. His In Lieu of Flowers, spring/summer 2027 collection, draws on the domestic interiors of Ghanaian households, using contemporary and traditional crafts as a cultural bridge.

Rising fashion star Tolu Coker is reimagining British tailoring through fusing her Nigerian heritage and her working-class upbringing in west London. Her February 2026 London Fashion Week presentation, which was attended by King Charles, took direct inspiration from the council estate where she grew up. The king’s presence was a significant moment of recognition for cultural value and Coker’s contribution to luxury fashion.

Elsewhere, debuting labels like are flourishing. NUB contemplates the convergence of heritage and metropolitan London life, while GOYAGOMA, founded by Traiceline Pratt, approaches womenswear through exploring identity, femininity and the everyday experiences of diasporic communities.

Storytelling and cultural reportage have themselves become a form of luxury. But this “luxury” is no longer just about expensive fabrics or high-end logos – instead, the real desirability and prestige come from the meaningful stories, history and authentic cultural heritage woven into the clothes.

At a time when immigration and national identity remain contested political questions, the work of these designers consolidates a vivid picture of modern Britain, shaped by overlapping cultures, communities and histories. Crucially, it offers a more expansive account of identity than political categories often allow.
Beyond a single Black aesthetic
History, experience and heritage remain central to storytelling. But designers are equally keen to debate how Black bodies should be dressed and understood.
More established voices like Bianca Saunders have already reworked traditional menswear silhouettes, challenging uncomfortable and familiar ideas about gender.

Saul Nash, also a choreographer and dancer, has assimilated technical sportswear with movement, helping to stage new expectations of masculinity – shaping a genderless, softer, fluid outcome. Nigerian-British designer Mowalola has been using a provocative design vocabulary to explore sexuality and popular culture with her distinctive use of leather, challenging gender expectations and respectable dress codes.

Jamaican-born and Cayman Islands-raised Jawara Alleyne’s experimental garments challenge commonplace notions of Black male bodies and masculinity. Through draping, slashing, knotting and pinning, his assembled propositions offer a unique culture clash of Caribbean traditions and London’s punk histories. Like many of his contemporaries, Alleyne’s education was completed at Central Saint Martins.

A 2019 graduate of University of the Arts London’s College of fashion, Abigail Ajobi uses luxury streetwear to engage with social issues, community empowerment and youth culture, intrinsically challenging the role of fashion and the runway.
A generation shaping Britain’s style future

Perhaps the most significant evolution is freedom to fearlessly author, build and create personal artistic worlds. Yaku Stapleton’s fantastical collections draw on family storytelling and creative character building influenced by video games. The designer imagines immersive environments which spawn playful, experimental clothing.

Torishéju Dumi also transforms her tailoring through experimental construction, drawing on historical references and unconventional silhouettes. Her work reflects on her personal cultural heritage, but she does not position it as its central purpose.

Ethiopian-born, London-based Feben approaches fashion through a surrealist lens, citing “form and matter” as merging contributors to distinctive textured and draped forms. Ronan McKenzie’s label, Selasi, works with the simple notion that women should “understand and listen to their own bodies” – and her cultural identity is embedded in the process.

In 2023, I co-curated The Missing Thread at Somerset House in London, an exhibition that recovered overlooked contributions to British fashion. One was Joe Casely-Hayford’s, which was shaped partly through responses to political and societal changes; at the same time, he defined the first iteration of Black British identity in fashion.

Today, this new generation is writing the next chapter while expanding into unexpected directions. Their work excels amid political tensions and arguments about immigration and belonging, but they are not necessarily presenting overt political statements. Being Black, or British, has never been a monolithic experience.

Culture is not fixed – it is a continuously altered by its participants. It is a tapestry to be refined, deconstructed and repurposed for its own users. These trailblazing young designers bring a huge range of voices to British fashion, expanding its cultural imagination and redefining who has the authority to construct and create identity.

articles.title: How London’s 1838 ‘great stink’ created the modern vampire
articles.author: Rae Gillibrand, Lecturer, Premodern History, University of Leeds
paras: Long before modern medicine could name the invisible terrors ravaging Victorian Britain, the public found a face for contagion: the vampire.

A new exhibition at the University of Leeds’s Treasures of the Brotherton Gallery, Quite Shameless: Cultural Reflections on the Vampire, explores how this supernatural predator became a stand-in for the period’s deepest anxieties about disease, contagion and contaminated air. The exhibition brings together manuscripts, books, prints, medical objects and theatrical materials, including items from the Bram Stoker collection.

Throughout the 19th century, rapid industrialisation brought huge numbers of people into British cities, where poverty, overcrowding and fragile infrastructure triggered devastating outbreaks of disease. As such, people were deeply concerned with questions of health and sanitation. However, knowledge of germ theory was not fully established until the end of the century and, in the meantime, people believed disease was spread by bad smells known as “miasma”.

In the summer of 1838, London experienced a heatwave that resulted in the “great stink”. The Thames was heavily polluted with rotting food, human waste and corpses of humans and animals. As temperatures soared, the river levels fell, leaving its contents to bake in the sun. The resulting cholera and typhoid epidemics were attributed to the terrible smell coming from the river, rather than the contaminated water supply.

These fears inspired John Leech’s illustration Silent Highwayman, published in Punch magazine in 1858 and on display in the exhibition. The cartoon presents a grim reaper like skeleton rowing through the bodies of dead animals in the shallow waters of the Thames. The caption, “your money or your life” demands that the government invest in public sanitation or risk losing more lives to disease.

Just as Leech presents disease through the personification of death, Bram Stoker did so through the character of the vampire. In his novel Dracula (1897), the titular vampire’s chambers contain a heavy miasma that is described by protagonist Jonathan Harker as “composed of all the ills of mortality and with the pungent, acrid smell of blood”.
However, bad smells weren’t the only explanation behind the spread of disease in the late-19th and early-20th centuries. People were also quick to blame migrants, travellers and foreigners.

An example of this in the exhibition can be seen in John Tenniel’s illustration, “Back!”. Published in Punch during the cholera outbreak of 1892, the drawing personifies cholera as a spectral figure attempting to enter Britain on a ship from abroad. Britannia holds out her hand, refusing entry to the migrant cholera, to prevent the spread of the disease into the country.
The cholera outbreaks of the 19th-century were a source of fear for their contemporaries. Over the course of the century, it is estimated that the disease killed about 140,000 people in the UK.

Stoker grew up in the shadow of this fear. His mother, Charlotte Thornley Stoker, had witnessed a devastating cholera outbreak as a teenager in her hometown of Sligo, Ireland. In just six weeks, about 640 local people had died. The blame fell on travellers who were believed to have brought the disease into the town. In her memoir, Thornley Stoker recounted the horrific treatment of one of these travellers:
One I vividly remember, a poor traveller was taken ill on the roadside […] [the people of Sligo] dug a pit and with long poles pushed him living into it and covered him up alive.

These stories of migrants targeted by fearful communities were formative for the young Bram Stoker and likely influenced his writing. Like his mother’s experiences with Cholera, Stoker’s villain Dracula is a traveller who enters a country at a port town, bringing a deadly and inexplicable disease with him. And, just like the cholera epidemics of the 1800s, the “disease” of vampirism is fought against by medical doctors. Most notably, in the case of Dracula, the Dutch medical doctor Abraham van Helsing and his former student Dr John Seward.
The representation of vampires as both migrants and bringers of disease becomes even more explicit in F.W. Murnau’s 1922 silent movie, Nosferatu.

In the film, Count Orlock (Max Schreck) travels from Transylvania to Germany on a ship infested with rats, bringing with him an unspecified disease known as “the great death”. While cholera was not spread by rats, the association between rats and disease was strong in the early-19th century mindset. The character design for Orlock is especially rodent-like, with elongated fangs resembling a rat’s prominent incisors.

For people in the 19th century, the vampire provided a way to make invisible threats visible. By transforming the transmission of disease into a literal monster, vampires make an intangible fear tangible and perhaps most importantly, into something that can be confronted.
Quite Shameless: Cultural Reflections on the Vampire is at the University of Leeds’ Treasures of the Brotherton Gallery. Tickets are free and the exhibition will run until May 29 2027.

articles.title: Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto turned architecture into horror’s greatest weapon
articles.author: Peter Nelson Lindfield, Lecturer in Architectural History, Cardiff University
paras: What does a haunted castle look like? Perhaps you imagine a ramshackle or imposing structure with towers, pinnacles and undefined spaces hidden in the shadows; some of its “prickly” gothic details picked out by moonlight. Threateningly ill-defined buildings, enough for our imagination to fill in the gaps, seem to be the ideal catalyst to spark terror.

Ever since the publication of Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto on Christmas Eve 1764, the novel has inspired visions of dark corridors, towering staircases, subterranean passages and moonlit chapels. The first novel to be identified as “gothic”, it’s presented as an ancient tale translated by the fictional William Marshal of Ghent.

Otranto cemented many of the themes that came to define the gothic literary genre: supernatural apparitions, family curses, ancient prophecies and mystery. Even so, one of the novel’s greatest achievements lies in an obscure character hidden in plain sight: the castle itself.
Woven throughout Otranto’s pages is a remarkable, changing architectural setting playing host to the novel’s action. The building, however, remains elusive.

You cannot draw a map of the castle because it is not mapped out in sufficient detail. This is despite Walpole, in the guise of Marshal, teasing readers in his preface to the first edition that it is “undoubtedly laid in some real castle”. He writes:

The author seems frequently, without design, to describe particular parts. The chamber, says he, on the right-hand; the door on the left-hand; the distance from the chapel to Conrad’s apartment: These and other passages are strong presumptions that the author had some certain building in his eye.

Perhaps it describes Walpole’s very own romantically styled gothic “castle”, really a country villa, in well-to-do Twickenham. Built across decades from 1749, Strawberry Hill recreated the architecture and sense of history found in Britain’s medieval cathedrals and homes. Strawberry Hill did not provide Otranto’s specific details. Instead, it helped shape the castle’s atmosphere: its dark passages, stained glass and carefully orchestrated contrasts of light and shadow embody what Walpole called “gloomth”.

This effect is certainly echoed in the novel’s castle setting, yet Otranto is not Strawberry Hill in disguise as often suggested. The novel’s architecture is stranger, less fixed and far more elusive than any real building.

Readers encounter Otranto’s architecture by degrees. Walpole never provides a complete description of the building nor its exact appearance. Instead, the castle emerges in fragments, glimpsed through moments of fear, wonder and supernatural disruption.
By refusing to pin down Otranto’s appearance and complete geography, Walpole encouraged generations of readers, artists and architects to imagine the castle for themselves.

Many drawings and paintings illustrating Otranto’s scenes were produced by fans of the novel. Those Walpole celebrated the most were produced in 1796, more than 30 years after the novel’s first publication, by teenage artist Bertie Greatheed Jr. Pasted into his personal copy of Otranto and today housed at Yale University’s Lewis Walpole Library in Connecticut, Walpole considered these watercolours the finest illustrations of his gothic story. He praised their ability to capture emotions and supernatural effects. On February 22 1796, Walpole wrote to the artist’s father.

I have seen many drawings and prints made from my idle […] not one of them approached to any one of your son’s four – a clear proof of which is, that not one of the rest satisfied the author’s ideas – It is as strictly, and upon my honour, true, that your son’s conception of some of the passions has improved them, and added more expression than I myself had formed in my own mind; for example, in the figure of the ghost in the chapel, to whose hollow sockets your son has given an air of reproachful anger, and to the whole turn of his person, dignity.

Beyond the figures’ deep psychological intensity, what makes these drawings so compelling is Greatheed’s use of tangible architectural settings. Rather than serving as passive gothic backdrops, the spaces actively drive the drama. Pointed arches frame terror and underline monstrous acts, vast interiors dwarf the figures and deep shadows hint at hidden dangers. By grounding the supernatural in believable, relatable architecture, Greatheed amplifies the emotional impact of each scene.

This relationship between architecture and fear lies at the heart of gothic fiction. Walpole believed medieval architecture possessed a unique capacity to stimulate the imagination. Gothic buildings, with their dramatic contrasts of light and dark, their hidden corners and soaring spaces, encouraged emotional responses that more orderly classical architecture rarely inspired. They could evoke awe, wonder, melancholy and terror.

Each Halloween, gothic architecture returns to popular culture in the form of haunted houses, castles, abbeys and ruins. Yet Walpole’s Castle of Otranto reminds us that the most unsettling gothic buildings are often those we cannot fully see. Like Greatheed’s illustrations, they leave enough hidden in shadow for the imagination to complete the picture.
